:::{#lem-nonneg-series}
#### Sums of non-negative terms

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ be values in $[0, \infty]$,
with partial sums $s_n$ (@def-partial-sum),
where $x + \infty = \infty$ for every $x$ in $[0, \infty]$.
Then the partial sums are [non-decreasing](#def-non-decreasing),
$s_1 \le s_2 \le \cdots$,
so their [limit](algebra.qmd#def-sequence-limit),
the infinite sum $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_i$ (@def-infinite-sum),
always exists,
and it is either a finite number or $\infty$.

:::

::: proof

For each $n$:

$$
\ba
s_{n+1}
&= s_n + a_{n+1}
&& \text{(definition of } s_{n+1} \text{)} \\
&\ge s_n
&& \text{(} a_{n+1} \ge 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

If some partial sum $s_N$ is $\infty$,
then $s_n = \infty$ for every $n \ge N$,
so the limit is $\infty$.
Otherwise, the partial sums form a non-decreasing sequence of [real numbers](notation.qmd#def-real-numbers).
If that sequence is [bounded above](algebra.qmd#def-bounded),
it [converges](algebra.qmd#def-sequence-limit) to a finite number
(see [Wikipedia: Monotone convergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monotone_convergence_theorem)).
If it is not bounded above,
then for every number $M$ some $s_N$ exceeds $M$,
and so does every later $s_n \ge s_N$;
the limit is $\infty$.

:::
